strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper convincingly argues that prior spatial 3DSGs and functional 3DSGs are complementary and incomplete, and the preliminary experiments in Fig. 2 (CLIP attention maps, GroundingDINO confidences) provide concrete evidence that open-vocabulary part grounding is a real bottleneck rather than an assumed one.

Meaningful system contribution: OP3DSG combines knowledge-guided entity-space control, color-distribution features for part association, and a geometry-initialized prior graph with verification-gated, decomposed LLM agents. The design choices are sensible, well explained, and each is individually validated in ablations (Table 5), which show non-trivial degradation when removed.

Valuable benchmark contribution (UniGraph3D): consolidating FunGraph3D and SceneFun3D with re-examined annotations, new object-part connectivity, and affordance labels addresses real annotation inconsistencies in prior datasets and enables the first systematic evaluation of unified 3DSG generation.

Strong empirical results with careful comparison design: the authors strengthen baselines by upgrading their LLM backbones (GPT-4 to GPT-5) and adding prompting, showing that the gains (+31 R@3 on part nodes, +9.2p functional triplets) do not merely stem from a stronger language model. Localization sensitivity analysis (Table 4) adds rigor beyond the lenient non-zero-IoU retrieval protocol.

End-to-end validation on a real Stretch3 robot (QA, task planning, navigation) demonstrates practical applicability of the representation beyond benchmark numbers, appropriate for an Applied/Systems-flavored contribution.
weaknesses: Benchmark scale and validation are limited: UniGraph3D contains only 251 object nodes and 414 part nodes from two existing ScanNet-derived datasets. There is no report of inter-annotator agreement or verification of the newly added affordance/part-connectivity labels, so the reliability of the ground truth that all conclusions rest on is hard to judge.

Dependence on a proprietary, non-reproducible LLM (GPT-5) for relation and affordance reasoning raises reproducibility and cost concerns; no runtime, API-cost, or latency analysis is provided even though efficiency/scalability is a central claimed advantage over VLM-captioning baselines.

The evaluation protocol deviates from prior work (BERT replaced by Sentence-BERT for relation matching), which is arguably better motivated but makes the reported numbers not directly comparable to previously published results; the leniency of embedding-similarity matching for relational phrases is not analyzed.

Part-level 3D localization remains weak (part IoU>=0.10 of 25.8 in Table 4, below KeySG's 30.4), meaning parts are largely recognized rather than geometrically grounded; the paper acknowledges this but the claim of 'fine-grained understanding' should be tempered accordingly.

Several components are heuristic and hand-tuned with limited analysis: an 'empirically curated' object-part knowledge base, a lexical containment rule for part-object attachment, a fixed 1-meter neighbor threshold, and multiple similarity weights (w^p, w^c_k, tau_S, tau_V) without sensitivity studies. This partly undercuts the open-vocabulary claim, since the entity space is steered by a closed, curated part list.

No explicit limitations or broader-impact discussion; generalization is untested beyond indoor scenes, and all baselines were extended by the authors themselves rather than evaluated on their original setups, which introduces some risk of inadvertently favoring the proposed pipeline.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: unifying spatial and functional 3DSGs into a single part-aware graph addresses a genuine gap in open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation for embodied AI, and the two challenges (part-level grounding difficulty, quadratic relation reasoning space) are clearly articulated.

The pipeline is coherently designed: knowledge-guided control of the entity space, part-aware multi-view fusion with color-distribution features, and geometry-initialized prior graphs with verification-gated LLM refinement form a sensible end-to-end system, and Fig. 2 provides a convincing motivating analysis of why off-the-shelf foundation models fail at part grounding.

The proposed UniGraph3D benchmark (consolidating FunGraph3D and SceneFun3D with re-examined annotations, object-part connectivity, and affordance labels) is a tangible community contribution beyond the method itself.

Comprehensive quantitative evaluation with strong margins (e.g., +31.2 R@3 part-node recall over the strongest baseline), a sensitivity study using stricter IoU/IoP thresholds, ablations covering each proposed component, and real-robot demonstrations (QA, task planning, navigation) on Stretch3 support the practical claims.
weaknesses: The 'open-vocabulary' claim is significantly weakened in practice: the entity space is steered by a 'pre-built object-part knowledge base, empirically curated to cover common object-part relations in indoor scenes'. This is effectively a closed, hand-curated prior for parts, so the framework is only open-vocabulary at the object level; the scope of applicability beyond indoor scenes and beyond the curated part inventory is unclear and not analyzed.

Reproducibility concerns: the method relies on proprietary LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-5), a specific open-vocabulary detector, and an empirically curated knowledge base whose contents and curation criteria are relegated to supplementary material. The heavy dependence on a closed-source, versioned LLM makes exact reproduction difficult and conflates method contributions with raw model capability, even with the GPT-4/GPT-5 baseline comparisons.

The evaluation protocol appears lenient and potentially favorable to the proposed method: node recall uses non-zero 3D IoU plus top-K label retrieval via CLIP embedding similarity, and the paper itself switches from BERT (prior work) to Sentence-BERT for relation matching. Only recall-style metrics are reported; no precision or graph-similarity measures are provided, so over-generation of nodes/edges is not penalized.

Under the stricter localization analysis (Table 4), part-node performance (25.8 IoU>=0.10, 13.0 IoP>=0.25) is actually below KeySG (30.4 / 23.4), despite part-aware perception being the central claim. The headline part-node gains rest largely on the lenient retrieval criterion, which the paper acknowledges but does not adequately reconcile with its claims.

The benchmark is small: 251 objects, 414 parts, and a few hundred edges consolidated from two existing datasets limits the statistical strength of the reported gains and the generality of conclusions; scene count and train/scene split details are not visible in the main paper.

Component-level novelty is limited: object association, point-cloud fusion, greedy matching, and feature updates closely follow ConceptGraphs, and the LLM reasoning is prompt engineering over a prior graph. The value is in system integration, but the paper is positioned as a general framework rather than an applied/systems contribution, and the assembly is not always justified against stronger alternatives.

Baselines are extended by the authors (ConceptGraph+*, OpenFunGraph with added prompting) and FunGraph/KeySG report 0.0 on functional triplets, making the edge comparison asymmetric; Open3DSG, the most relevant open-vocabulary 3DSG method in related work, is absent from the comparison.

Claims about efficiency (avoiding VLM captioning overhead, scalability beyond O(N^2)) are made repeatedly but never quantified; no runtime, token-cost, or scaling-curve measurements are provided, and qualitative results are limited to partial regions of two scenes.

Robot applications are anecdotal demonstrations without quantitative success rates or comparisons, so the claim that unified graphs serve as a 'strong perception backbone' for downstream tasks is only weakly evidenced.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: unifying spatial and functional 3DSGs into a single part-aware graph addresses a genuine gap in embodied perception, and Fig. 2 provides convincing preliminary evidence for why part-centric open-vocabulary grounding is intrinsically hard.

Concrete and sensible technical design: the geometry-initialized prior graph combined with verification-gated, decomposed LLM agents is a plausible and effective way to tame the combinatorial explosion of relation prediction, and the ablation (Table 5) shows each component contributes meaningfully—especially the knowledge-guided entity control and the split-agent design.

A new benchmark (UniGraph3D) consolidating FunGraph3D and SceneFun3D with refined annotations, expanded part/affordance labels, and multiple evaluation protocols (node, triplet, affordance, localization sensitivity) is a useful community contribution.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough: comparisons against multiple recent baselines under both GPT-4 and GPT-5 backbones help isolate gains attributable to structure rather than the LLM, and the localization sensitivity analysis (Table 4) honestly reveals residual part-localization weakness.
End-to-end validation on a real Stretch3 robot for QA, task planning, and navigation demonstrates practical applicability beyond benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: The open-vocabulary claim is partially undermined by the pre-built, empirically curated object-part knowledge base K, which restricts part candidates to a predefined indoor taxonomy; this is effectively a closed part vocabulary layered on top of open-vocabulary object detection, and the paper does not discuss the limits this imposes on novel/unseen part types.

UniGraph3D is small (251 objects, 414 parts across a limited set of indoor scenes), so the large reported margins (+31pp part-node recall) come from a modest testbed; no variance/significance analysis is provided, and the benchmark doubles as the authors' own evaluation suite, which risks overfitting method design to the dataset (e.g., lexical containment heuristics aligned with their own annotation conventions).

Heavy dependence on a proprietary LLM (GPT-5) for relation and affordance inference raises reproducibility, cost, and long-term availability concerns; the ablation showing a dramatic drop without the split-agent design (Table 5) suggests sensitivity to prompt engineering that is not analyzed in the main text.

Baseline adaptation fairness: OP3DSG uses a part-centric pretrained detector [41] plus a curated knowledge base, while baselines are given only generic LLM prompts; part of the part-node gain may stem from the stronger specialized detector rather than the framework itself, and this is not disentangled in the ablations.

The main node metric uses non-zero 3D IoU, a very lenient overlap criterion; the stricter IoU≥0.10/IoP≥0.25 results (Table 4) show notably lower part-node numbers (25.8/13.0), and while acknowledged, this gap deserves more prominent treatment relative to headline claims.

Scalability claims rest on a fixed 1-meter neighbor threshold and a small number of scenes; behavior in larger, cluttered, or multi-room environments is untested. The manuscript is also light on implementation details in the main text (thresholds τ_S, τ_V, w^p, α, prompts deferred to supplementary), and the limitations discussion is brief (one sentence on part localization), with no runtime/latency comparison despite criticizing VLM-captioning pipelines for overhead.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: the paper convincingly argues that existing open-vocabulary 3DSG pipelines are object-centric while functional 3DSGs lack spatial structure, and it defines a concrete Unified 3DSG task (objects, parts, spatial/functional relations, affordances) that is genuinely useful for embodied reasoning. Fig. 2's preliminary analysis of CLIP/GroundingDINO failure on part-centric prompts is a nice motivating study.

Three-pronged contribution: a task formulation, a method (OP3DSG), and a benchmark (UniGraph3D). Each is substantive: the knowledge-guided entity-space control addresses part grounding, the color-distribution features address part association during fusion, and the geometry-initialized prior graph with verification-gated, decomposed LLM agents is a sensible design that scales relation inference beyond O(N^2) enumeration.

Comprehensive experimental evidence: comparisons against multiple baselines including versions upgraded to GPT-5 (which controls for the stronger LLM backbone), ablations isolating every major component (knowledge base, color features, prior graph, split LLM agents), a localization sensitivity study with stricter IoU/IoP thresholds, efficiency analysis, per-dataset breakdowns (Tables 8-9), and generalization to object-centric evaluation on ReplicaSSG.

UniGraph3D benchmark consolidation is valuable: human re-annotation, label normalization of ambiguous functional relation phrases (Table 10), expanded part/relation/affordance annotations, and documented annotation procedures—this addresses real evaluation inconsistencies in prior datasets.

Real-world demonstration on a Stretch3 robot across QA, task planning, text query/navigation, plus honest failure-case analysis (fragmented nodes, mirror reflections, thin-object misclassification) in the supplement.
weaknesses: Strong dependence on a proprietary, closed-source GPT-5 model for reasoning harms reproducibility and makes exact replication of headline numbers impossible; while the GPT-5 ('++') baseline upgrades are appreciated, results may not transfer to open LLMs, and no open-model comparison is reported.

The 'open-vocabulary' claim is partially undermined by the empirically curated object-part knowledge base K, which pre-defines plausible parts per detected object category; coverage for unseen object categories and sensitivity to K's construction are not analyzed.

Benchmark scale is modest (~251 object nodes, 414 part nodes across scenes from two source datasets); conclusions about multi-level relational reasoning would be more convincing with broader scene coverage or additional datasets, and node evaluation depends on top-K CLIP retrieval with non-zero-IoU matching, a relatively permissive criterion.

The evaluation protocol change (BERT to Sentence-BERT for relation matching) and author-extended baselines (added part/functional inference to ConceptGraph, spatial inference to OpenFunGraph) mean numbers are not directly comparable to prior literature; although the authors motivate this, there is residual risk that baseline extensions are weaker than native implementations.

Several design choices feel heuristic and under-analyzed: the 1-meter neighbor radius for prior-graph edges, lexical containment for part-object attachment (brittle to label phrasing), fixed similarity weights (w_c, w^p) and thresholds with no sensitivity analysis or cross-dataset validation of these hyperparameters.

Part-node geometric localization remains weak even for the proposed method (Table 4: IoU>=0.10 R@3 of 25.8), acknowledged by the authors but not addressed; the gap between semantic retrieval success and true 3D grounding quality deserves more investigation given the paper's emphasis on physical interaction.

Missing comparison against dedicated part-level 3D perception baselines (e.g., lifting-oriented approaches like PartSLIP++, Find3D, SAMPart3D), which would strengthen the claim that the fusion pipeline is the right way to ground parts in 3D.

No dedicated limitations discussion in the main paper, and no runtime/latency figures for the LLM reasoning stage despite claims of scalability (Table 6 reports call counts but not wall-clock or cost, which matter given the multi-agent GPT-5 design).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing open-vocabulary 3DSG methods are object-centric, and the proposed Unified 3DSG formulation (objects + parts + spatial/functional relations + affordances) is a sensible target for embodied reasoning.

The UniGraph3D benchmark is a useful community contribution: it consolidates SceneFun3D and FunGraph3D under a normalized annotation schema, adds spatial relations and affordance annotations, and the label-consolidation analysis in the supplement (Table 10) is thoughtful.

Experimental coverage is broad: main comparison with strengthened baselines (GPT-5 variants), ablations of all major components, localization-sensitivity analysis with stricter IoU/IoP thresholds, per-dataset results, ReplicaSSG generalization, efficiency analysis, and real-robot demonstrations on Stretch3.

The geometry-initialized prior graph with verification-gated LLM refinement is a reasonable design for making LLM reasoning tractable, and the ablations (especially 'w/o split LLM') support the claim that decomposed, constrained reasoning matters beyond a stronger backbone.
Failure cases are discussed honestly (Fig. 6 and Sec. A.4), including the acknowledged weakness of part-node geometric localization in Table 4.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the framework is largely an integration of existing components (RAM for tagging, VLPart for detection, SAM for masks, color-histogram association, GPT-5 for reasoning). The knowledge-guided entity-space control rests on a manually 'empirically curated' object-part knowledge base K, which arguably contradicts the open-vocabulary claim—part recognition is restricted to predefined object-part pairs, and the paper does not report the coverage or size of K, nor behavior on parts outside K.

Evaluation metrics are recall-only and lenient: the main node protocol uses non-zero 3D IoU plus top-K CLIP similarity, and edges/affordances are matched by Sentence-BERT cosine similarity without any precision metric. Recall-only evaluation can favor methods that over-generate nodes and edges, which is precisely the failure mode (spurious relations) the LLM component is claimed to suppress; the paper never verifies that claim quantitatively. The Table 4 result that part-node IoU>=0.10 (25.8) actually falls below KeySG (30.4) despite a +31 point recall gain under non-zero IoU suggests the headline gains may be substantially inflated by the lenient protocol.

The benchmark is small (251 objects, 414 parts, 357/425 edges across a handful of indoor scenes) and no inter-annotator agreement or annotation-quality statistics are reported, despite the paper's core argument being that prior annotations were inconsistent. The similarity-threshold-based annotation consolidation itself could bias toward methods using similar phrasing.

Heavy dependence on a proprietary, closed LLM (GPT-5) with multiple agentic calls raises reproducibility and cost concerns; the actual prompts, number of calls per scene, and variance across LLM runs are not reported in the main text. Ablations do not examine sensitivity to the LLM backbone beyond the ++ baseline rows.

The motivation experiment (Fig. 2) uses CLIP and GroundingDINO, but the method adopts VLPart pretrained on LVIS/PACO; the preliminary analysis therefore does not directly justify the design choice, and a comparison against part-centric detectors without the full pipeline is missing.

The 'open-vocabulary' framing is strained: the paper evaluates on datasets whose parts and relations derive from the same ScanNet-derived scenes and curated label sets that informed the knowledge base, so generalization to genuinely novel part vocabularies or outdoor/dynamic environments is untested.

Several implementation details needed for reproduction (association thresholds, prompt lists, vote-based label selection details, knowledge base contents) are deferred or absent; given the pipeline is training-free, full prompt/spec release is essential and only partially evidenced.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly articulated gap: existing open-vocabulary 3D scene graph methods are object-centric and cannot support fine-grained embodied reasoning that requires part-level grounding, functional relations, and affordances. The 'Unified 3D Scene Graph' formulation is a sensible and useful problem contribution.

The UniGraph3D benchmark is a genuine contribution beyond a simple dataset merge: annotation inconsistencies across SceneFun3D and FunGraph3D were identified and consolidated into canonical labels, object-part spatial relations and affordance annotations were added, and per-dataset evaluations (Tables 8-9) verify the gains are not artifacts of the merged benchmark.

The core technical insight—that geometry can serve as a strong prior making open-vocabulary part-aware reasoning tractable—is well-executed: the geometry-initialized prior graph plus verification-gated LLM refinement is a sound design that converts unconstrained LLM generation into constrained refinement, addressing both scalability (avoiding O(N^2) pair enumeration) and hallucination.

Comprehensive and fair experimental evidence: baselines are strengthened with additional prompting and a GPT-5 backbone so that gains cannot be attributed to a stronger language model alone; ablations (Table 5) cleanly isolate each component; localization sensitivity analysis (Table 4) reveals honest limitations in part-node geometric accuracy; efficiency analysis (Table 6) shows reduced memory and LLM calls versus VLM-captioning baselines; and generalization to the object-centric ReplicaSSG setting is demonstrated.

Real-world validation on a Stretch3 robot with multiple downstream tasks (QA, task planning, navigation) supports the claim that the unified graph is a usable perception backbone, and the qualitative failure-case analysis (occlusion, reflections, thin objects) is candid and informative.

The preliminary motivating experiments (Fig. 2) convincingly demonstrate that part-centric prompts fail with CLIP/GroundingDINO, grounding the paper's claims about intrinsic difficulty of part-level open-vocabulary grounding.
weaknesses: The framework is largely an integration of existing components (RAM tagging, VLPart, SAM, GPT-5) with hand-crafted heuristics rather than a new learning algorithm; several design choices are ad hoc—the 'empirically curated' object-part knowledge base K risks dataset-specific bias (it may implicitly encode the benchmark's object/part vocabulary), and the lexical heuristic for part-object attachment (object label contained within part label text) is brittle for open-vocabulary settings.

Reproducibility concerns: the pipeline depends on GPT-5 (gpt-5-2025-08-07), a closed, versioned, non-deterministic API whose behavior may change or be withdrawn; results obtained with a proprietary frontier model are hard to reproduce exactly, and the paper does not report variance across repeated LLM runs or API cost.

The evaluation protocol is relatively lenient for node retrieval: a non-zero 3D IoU is the only spatial consistency filter in the main tables, which favors methods that over-segment; while Table 4 addresses this with stricter thresholds, part-node performance under strict IoU (25.8) lags behind KeySG (30.4), indicating the headline part-node gains come substantially from semantic retrieval rather than geometric accuracy. Also, only recall-based metrics are reported; no precision or F1-style metric exists to quantify spurious nodes/edges, despite hallucination suppression being a central claim.

The benchmark is small (251 objects, 414 parts, ~425 functional edges, derived from SceneFun3D/FunGraph3D scenes), so the large margins in Tables 2-3 could partly reflect annotation noise or limited scene diversity; inter-annotator agreement statistics for the new affordance/connectivity annotations are not reported.

Several methodological details are underspecified: the association thresholds for the greedy fusion, the NNR definition parameters, the remotable-candidate selection procedure for the remote-relation agent, and the Sentence-BERT similarity threshold for relation matching are not given in the main text; these affect reproducibility.

Scalability claims (e.g., 'ensuring scalability as the number of nodes increases') are argued rather than empirically demonstrated with graphs of varying size; the efficiency comparison (Table 6) compares peak GPU memory of the detection stage only, and the O(1) LLM-call claim (> 3 calls) is not stress-tested on large scenes.

No discussion of failure modes of the LLM reasoning agents themselves (e.g., wrong remote-relation pairings propagating through downstream planning) and no societal-impact discussion, though this is minor given the scope.
